summary: Rodent efficacy studies frequently report positive effects in animals but these often fail to predict human benefit. O'Collins et al. 2006 found 62% of focal‑ischemia experimental results were superior to control and Ritskes‑Hoitinga et al. 2022 found 82% of preclinical studies in investigator brochures reported positive findings, yet Mak et al. 2014 estimated <8% average translation from animal cancer models to successful clinical trials and Martić‑Kehl et al. 2012 identified only 3 of 494 animal‑positive stroke interventions with convincing patient benefit. Some areas show successful translation (e.g., three alcohol medications; concordant DKD effects for ACEi/ARB, SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP‑1RAs) and dose‑range overlap can be high (Ferreira et al. 2023 reported 84% HED overlap), but overall results are variable and context‑dependent.
why_range_is_wide: Reported translation rates vary widely across therapeutic areas, study quality and reporting practices; Ritskes‑Hoitinga et al. 2022 explicitly reported translation rates ranging 0–100%, reflecting heterogeneity in indication, design, and selective/publication bias.

summary: Evidence is mixed: some primate efficacy findings translated to humans (Perel et al. 2007 report thrombolysis reduced infarct volume in animal models by 24% and improved neurobehavioural scores by 23%; Banks et al. 2017 and Spanagel 2017 report concordant results for d‑amphetamine and three alcohol medications), while other primate-positive interventions failed in patients (Perel et al. 2007 and Pound et al. 2018 note corticosteroids and tirilazad showed animal benefit but no clinical benefit). Quantitatively, failures can be large: Martić‑Kehl et al. 2012 found only 3 of 494 animal‑positive stroke interventions produced convincing patient benefit and report 100% prediction failure for chimpanzee/macaque AIDS vaccine models. Pharmacokinetic/dose comparisons give a more positive picture for exposure prediction (Ferreira et al. 2023 found mean HED overlap 84% and 72% of studies had ≥80% HED overlap), but Ferreira also reports that 36% of clinical studies exceeded the animal NOAEL for HED and 16% had unacceptable side effects below the NOAEL, and Pound et al. 2018 found <7% of studies met ethical permissibility criteria.
why_range_is_wide: Reported performance varies by outcome type and intervention class (e.g., thrombolysis and some addiction treatments vs vaccines and corticosteroids/Tirilazad), by endpoint (pathology vs behaviour vs vaccine protection vs PK/exposure metrics), and by study selection: Ferreira et al. 2023 analysed a small, selected set of 25 IBs, which may inflate apparent dose‑overlap concordance.

summary: Evidence shows mouse efficacy studies give inconsistent predictions of human efficacy: some pooled animal results tracked clinical findings (Perel et al. 2007 found thrombolysis reduced infarct volume by 24% and improved neurobehavioural scores by 23%, and bisphosphonates increased bone mineral density by ~11% in the hip and ~8.5% in the spine), and alcohol models contributed to three approved medications (Spanagel et al. 2017). However, other analyses found little or no predictive value — Perrin et al. 2014 reports that for nine ALS candidates published mouse studies showed 10–35% survival gains while rigorous ALS TDI mouse studies showed 0% and all compounds failed in humans, and Pan et al. 2020 found tumor growth inhibition (TGI) in mouse models had AUC = 0.45 (worse than chance) with medians 0.74 vs 0.77 (p=0.375). Pound et al. 2018 further noted that fewer than 7% of studies met permissibility criteria and documented both concordant and discordant intervention-specific outcomes, so predictive performance is highly context- and quality-dependent.
why_range_is_wide: Reported effect sizes vary by disease area, intervention and study quality: for example Perrin et al. 2014 contrasts 10–35% survival gains in published ALS mouse studies with 0% in ALS TDI’s more rigorous replications; Perel and Pan syntheses aggregate many different models and outcomes, so ranges reflect heterogeneity of interventions, endpoints, and methodological rigor.

summary: Evidence from rat efficacy studies is mixed: some rat results tracked human outcomes (e.g., thrombolysis in rats reduced infarct volume by 24% and improved neurobehavioural scores by 23%, Perel et al. 2007; three alcohol medications developed using rat models later reached the clinic, Spanagel 2017; d-amphetamine effects in rat choice procedures matched human laboratory/clinical findings, Banks et al. 2017). Other rat findings did not translate (corticosteroids showed a pooled odds ratio of 0.58 for reduced adverse functional outcome in animal head‑injury models but showed no clinical benefit, Perel et al. 2007; tirilazad reduced infarct volume by 29% and improved neurobehavioural scores by 48% in animals yet was discordant with human outcomes, Perel et al. 2007; Pound et al. 2018 categorised corticosteroids, tirilazad and antifibrinolytics as discordant). Overall the data show selective concordance depending on intervention and outcome measure.
why_range_is_wide: Reported effects span different interventions and different outcome types (e.g., infarct volume vs neurobehavioural scores) and come from pooled meta-analyses that aggregate many experiments of varying design, so the magnitude varies by intervention, outcome metric, and study-level heterogeneity.

summary: Sheep efficacy data are mixed. Animal thrombolysis studies showed reduced infarct volume (24% reduction) and improved neurobehavioural scores (23%) that aligned with clinical benefit, and alendronate increased bone mineral density in hip (11.0%) and lumbar spine (8.5%) — findings judged concordant (Perel et al. 2007; Pound et al. 2018). In contrast, several interventions diverged from human outcomes: corticosteroids reduced adverse functional outcome in animal head‑injury models (pooled odds ratio 0.58) but not clinically, tirilazad reduced infarct volume by 29% and improved neurobehavioural scores by 48% in animals yet failed in trials, and antenatal corticosteroids markedly increased neonatal mortality in ewes (odds ratio 12.5) (Perel et al. 2007; Pound et al. 2018). Pound et al. 2018 also reported that fewer than 7% of studies met permissibility criteria, which raises ethical and methodological concerns about study conduct and interpretability.
why_range_is_wide: Reported effects span different interventions and outcomes (e.g., infarct volume and neurobehavioural scores for stroke drugs, bone mineral density for bisphosphonates, and neonatal mortality for antenatal corticosteroids), and concordance with human results varies by intervention and by the outcome measured.

summary: The data show dog toxicology findings give modest, endpoint-dependent information about human toxicity: combined rat+dog regulatory tests matched human toxicities in 71% of cases (Jang et al. 2019), but dog-only performance is inconsistent. A negative dog test raises the estimated probability of no human toxicity to ~72% (Bailey et al. 2019), while dog median PPV was 0.67 and NPV 0.52 for all toxicity grades (Atkins et al. 2020) and the dog inverse NLR is near unity (1.10; Bailey et al. 2015), implying little evidential weight from absence. For some specific endpoints dog results track human outcomes better (dog LR+ for cardiac disorders 6.11; Clark et al. 2018), so predictive value depends strongly on endpoint and study method.
why_range_is_wide: Reported performance varies because studies mix endpoints (all grades vs grade 3–4), aggregate species (rats+dogs) versus dog-only analyses, and different metrics (PPV/NPV, LR, iNLR). Compound-specific effects and assay types (in vivo regulatory studies vs in vitro Liver-Chips) produce large, endpoint-specific differences (e.g., JNJ‑3 potency 3–10× dog versus human in Jang et al. 2019).

summary: Across five studies the evidence is mixed: non-human primate (NHP) toxicology sometimes tracked human outcomes for specific organs/endpoints (e.g. Monticello et al. 2017 reported an 83% PPV for nervous-system findings and Clark et al. 2018 reported LR+ up to 11 for hepatobiliary disorders in cynomolgus monkeys), but overall predictive value was limited (Monticello et al. 2017 overall PPV 43% and sensitivity 48%, and Bailey et al. 2019 found the probability of no human toxicity after a negative NHP test was only 70.4%). Atkins et al. 2020 and Bailey et al. 2015/2019 emphasise low-to-moderate median PPVs/NPVs and inverse likelihood ratios close to 1, indicating little overall evidential weight from NHPs for ruling in or ruling out human toxicity.
why_range_is_wide: Reported performance varies by metric, dataset and endpoint: some analyses use overall PPV/sensitivity (lower values), others report organ- or endpoint-specific measures (e.g. nervous-system PPV or LR+ for hepatobiliary/ cardiac) that are much higher. Differences also arise from toxicity grade (all grades vs grade 3–4), low clinical prevalence inflating NPVs, and selection bias in datasets (marketed drugs or compounds that progressed to NHP testing).

summary: Evidence shows rodent toxicology findings tracked human organ toxicities inconsistently: rodent-only concordance/sensitivity clustered around 43–48% (Wall et al. 2008 found rodent models correctly predicted human organ toxicity in 43% of 150 compounds; Monticello et al. 2017 reported overall sensitivity 48%; Olson et al. 2000 reported rodents alone predicted 43% of human toxicities). The chance that an animal toxicity indicated a human adverse event was modest (mean PPV ~36% in Bailey et al. 2019; 43% PPV reported by Monticello et al. 2017), and a negative animal result did not guarantee absence of human toxicity (~74% probability of no human toxicity given no animal toxicity in Bailey et al. 2019). Performance varied by organ and by whether rodent data were combined with nonrodent data: Olson et al. 2000 reported 91% concordance for hematologic findings and a combined rodent+nonrodent true‑positive concordance of ~71%.
why_range_is_wide: Estimates vary because studies differ in scope and metrics (rodent-only versus combined rodent+nonrodent analyses), organ-specific performance (e.g., hematologic 91% vs much lower for cutaneous), clinical prevalence and trial phase (which affect PPV/NPV), and selection bias in some datasets (Olson et al. 2000 included only compounds with identified human toxicities).

summary: Evidence is mixed: rat toxicity findings sometimes track human outcomes but only modestly and variably. Atkins et al. 2020 found a median positive predictive value (PPV) of 0.65 and median negative predictive value (NPV) of 0.50 for animal toxicity overall (rat values reported in those medians), while Clark et al. 2018 reports rat likelihood ratios that raise post-test odds modestly (LR+ 2.74 for hepatobiliary and LR+ 4.73 for cardiac disorders). Bailey et al. 2015 reports a rat iNLR of 1.82, meaning absence of a finding in rat studies only weakly decreases the odds of human toxicity, and Jang et al. 2019 notes that regulatory testing in rats and dogs together correctly predicted 71% of human toxicities but gives species-specific examples where rat assays missed human-relevant signals.
why_range_is_wide: Numbers come from different metrics, endpoints and datasets: some are combined rat+dog summaries (71% from Jang et al.), some are medians across grades or species (Atkins), some are organ-specific likelihood ratios (Clark), and others measure evidential weight of negative results (Bailey). Predictive performance therefore varies by toxicity grade, organ system and whether results are pooled across species.

summary: Overall, the evidence shows mouse toxicology findings do not reliably predict human toxicities: mouse positive findings only modestly match human events while absence of findings provides little reassurance. Atkins et al. 2020 reported a mouse median PPV of 0.57 for all toxicity grades (fraction of mouse-predicted toxicities observed in humans) and a PPV of 0.43 for grade 3–4 toxicities, though NPV for grade 3–4 was 0.81 (fraction of mouse-negative severe-toxicity results also negative in humans). Clark et al. 2018 found some endpoint-specific signal (mouse LR+ 5.29 for cardiac disorders, an increase in odds of a human cardiac event when mice show a finding), but overall selectivity across species/endpoints was low; Bailey et al. 2015 gave a mouse median iNLR of 1.39, indicating that animal absence of toxicity provides essentially no evidential weight for absence in humans.

summary: Across three studies, zebrafish toxicology assays generally tracked mammalian toxicology outcomes. McGrath et al. 2008 identified all tested teratogens (100%) and correctly classified 75% of non‑teratogens; Nikam et al. 2020 reported 100% concordance with mammalian screening overall, 100% concordance for hepatotoxicity and 90% agreement for teratogenicity (59 compounds); Cornet et al. 2017 found the ZeGlobalTox platform had 78% overall accuracy with overall specificity 89% and sensitivity 68%. summary: Overall, dog (large-animal) cardiovascular findings generally track human QTc and combined BP/HR results but not perfectly: 91% of drugs that prolonged QT in humans also prolonged QT in nonrodent animals, and large-animal to human concordance for combined BP/HR showed sensitivity ~78% and specificity ~79% (Valentin et al. 2022; Bhatt et al. 2019). Dog-specific discrimination for clinical QT outcome was good by ROC (AUC 0.81 overall, 0.91 when two β2-agonists were excluded; Pollard et al. 2017), and a PK–PD example (moxifloxacin) gave a canine QTc increase of 16.6 ms versus ~10 ms in humans with similar C‑QTc slopes (Sadko et al. 2024). However, substantial discordance appears in some datasets (31% discordant of 150 drugs and 65% nonclinical false negatives among TQT‑positive drugs in Valentin et al. 2022), so negative and false‑negative results can occur depending on assay and exposure conditions.
why_range_is_wide: Estimates vary because studies pool different endpoints (QTc vs BP vs HR), use different assays and exposure multiples (sensitivity rose with higher exposure), and sometimes exclude specific drug classes (e.g., β2‑agonists); predictive values also depend on the prevalence of positives in each dataset.
negative_controls: Sadko et al. 2024 included a vehicle/mock negative control that produced no QTc increase in canines (reported ~0.04 ms), which validated assay specificity.

Bhatt et al. 2019 found rats predicted combined blood-pressure/heart-rate effects seen in larger species (84% sensitivity, 71% specificity for combined BP/HR) but 23–26% of drugs produced the opposite direction for HR or BP. summary: Baldrick et al. 2021 shows that non-rodent conscious telemetry identified drug-induced QTc interval changes in about 10% of telemetry studies (10% of studies) and that in vivo cardiovascular (conscious telemetry) testing was the primary non-rodent modality that provided utility for supporting safe clinical entry. At the same time the authors report that a stand-alone hERG assay was not "particularly sensitive" for predicting proarrhythmic risk and that low hERG IC50 values (e.g., ≤1 µM) showed little correlation with animal cardiovascular data. Taken together, non-rodent telemetry sometimes tracked electrophysiological signals relevant to safety (QTc in ~10% of studies) but in vitro hERG measurements did not reliably predict those animal cardiovascular findings.

summary: Evidence is mixed: several studies report clear transcriptomic agreement between specific mouse models and the corresponding human disease (e.g. Takao et al. 2015 found Spearman r = 0.43–0.68 and 77–93% of genes changing in the same direction), and disease‑focused models show large overlapping DEG sets (Hansen et al. 2020 found 4,418 overlapping DEGs between GAN DIO‑NASH mice and human NASH). However, other analyses find little or near‑random correspondence — for example Seok et al. 2013 reported very low Pearson R^2 (≤0.09) with only ~47–63% of genes changing in the same direction, and Kodamullil et al. 2017 reported that mouse models mimicked only 12% of genes deregulated in human conditions. Overall, whether mouse results “track” human disease depends strongly on the model, analytic threshold and the metric used.
why_range_is_wide: Reported concordance varies by disease model, timepoint/duration, data thresholding and metric: some papers compare top/high‑magnitude genes or pathway enrichment (raising correlations), others use whole‑transcriptome Pearson/Spearman on all orthologs (lower correlations), and exposure duration or diet/model protocol substantially changes recall/overlap.

summary: Rat data track human disease biology for many physiological and behavioural readouts but diverge for some transcriptomic and pharmacologic responses. For example, 26/30 blood biochemical variables changed in the same direction after exercise and the magnitude of uniform change was similar (7.9% in rats vs 7.3% in humans; Goutianos et al. 2015), and cognitive/electrophysiological task patterns were comparable (rats 2.6 vs humans 4.4 reversals/100 trials; Der-Avakian et al. 2025). By contrast, transcriptomic concordance in Parkinson’s disease models is poor (average concordance in rat PD studies = -0.04 and animal models recovered 10% of PD-associated genes vs 36% in human studies; Oerton et al. 2017), and rats showed divergence under some interventions (10/19 biomarkers had species×vitamin C interactions; Veskoukis et al. 2016).
why_range_is_wide: Estimates vary because studies measure different endpoints and models: acute physiological assays and behavioural/electrophysiological tasks (exercise biomarkers, cognitive tasks) show close rat–human agreement, whereas transcriptomic meta-analyses (Parkinson’s models) and certain pharmacologic manipulations (vitamin C) show poor concordance; disease model, assay type, and experimental manipulation drive the heterogeneity.

summary: Evidence is mixed. Tarandovskiy et al. 2020 report coagulation parameters in baboon and rhesus that are close to human values (e.g., rhesus thrombin production 111.22 nM/min vs human 111.51 nM/min), and Ranjan et al. 2025 argue structural/neurodevelopmental features favour primates for some disease biology. However, Marshall et al. 2023 found 67–80% of non-human primate trials showed apparent improvement while only 32% of human trials showed clinical improvement, and Oerton et al. 2017 report that animal-model meta-analysis recovered 10% of PD-associated genes versus 36% from human studies—together indicating animal (including NHP) findings do not consistently track human disease biology.
why_range_is_wide: The 67–80% range for non-human primate trials (Marshall et al. 2023) reflects different NHP trial subsets/definitions reported within that study (e.g., varying disease areas or inclusion criteria), not a single pooled estimate.

summary: Evidence shows pigs partially recapitulate human coagulation: Tarandovskiy et al. 2020 measured a swine thrombin concentration peak of 242.35 nM (≈50% of the human 484.25 nM) and a thrombin production rate of 93.6 nM/min (≈84% of the human 111.51 nM), but swine samples produced no detectable plasmin while human plasmin peak is 457.20 nM and production rate 34.80 nM/min. Ranjan et al. 2025 highlights general limitations of animal models for human disease biology and favors primate models for some neurodevelopmental traits, providing no evidence that pigs reproduce human-specific transcriptional or neurodevelopmental features. Overall, pig results partly track human thrombin metrics but fail to reproduce human fibrinolysis, so translatability for disease biology is mixed.

summary: Zong et al. 2023 shows D. melanogaster transcriptomes have small, inconsistent similarity to inflammatory signatures: most within‑stage cross‑species genome‑wide c‑scores involving Drosophila exceeded 0.1, but at least one stage pair (C. elegans larva vs D. melanogaster larva) was 0.087. The paper reports human–human genome‑wide c‑scores up to 0.25–0.52 for some comparisons and ≈0 for others, so Drosophila’s c‑scores are generally much lower than the highest human–human concordances. Overall the evidence is mixed: D. melanogaster tracks some stage‑matched transcriptomic signals but only with small overlaps to human inflammatory profiles.
why_range_is_wide: Values come from different pairwise and sub‑analyses: (a) within‑stage cross‑species comparisons (Drosophila vs other species) cluster just above 0.1, (b) specific human–human pathway comparisons reach 0.25–0.52, and (c) other human pairs show c‑scores ≈0; the reported range therefore reflects different species pairs, stages, and pathway‑level versus genome‑wide tests.

summary: Oreff et al. 2021 shows that horse tenocyte responses match human tenocytes under transient inflammatory conditions (Mahalanobis distance for all genes = 9.59) and that horses approximate human wound-closure/migration, but horse baseline (healthy) proliferation differs markedly from human (slope difference to human = 0.3000, p<2e-16). Proliferation difference under transient inflammation was small and not significant (slope = 0.0233, p=0.4868), while migration differences were small (migration slope difference under healthy = 0.0133, p=0.00375). Overall, similarity depends on the inflammatory context and on which gene sets are considered.
why_range_is_wide: Similarity metrics vary by inflammatory condition (e.g., all-genes Mahalanobis distance 23.05 in healthy vs 9.59 in transient inflammation) and by gene subset (e.g., MMPs distance 4.65 vs inflammatory mediators 17.77), so different sub-analyses yield the wide range of values.

summary: Oreff et al. 2021 shows sheep tenocyte gene-expression profiles best match human tenocytes under constant inflammation (Mahalanobis distance 8.94 for all genes) but are much less similar under healthy conditions (distance 24.78). Sheep also show condition-dependent differences in measured behaviors: proliferation slope differed from human under healthy (slope difference 0.1169, p=1.10e-06, n=3) and under constant inflammation (slope difference −0.0878, p=0.009, n=3); migration slope differences were smaller (e.g. −0.0188 vs human under transient inflammation, p=0.00374, n=3). Overall, gene-expression similarity favors sheep only in the constant-inflammation setting while functional readouts (proliferation/migration) show mixed concordance with human.
why_range_is_wide: Values vary across inflammatory conditions (healthy vs transient vs constant) and across gene subsets (all genes, MMPs, collagens, tenogenic markers), so similarity spans ~8.9–24.8 depending on condition and gene set.

summary: Evidence is mixed. Petersen-Jones et al. 2015 found dog RPE65 gene‑therapy outcomes did NOT track human clinical outcomes: dogs showed restored ERG and vision near normal while human patients showed no ERG change, remained visually impaired, and had much greater photoreceptor loss (degree of rescue in humans “nowhere near” that in dogs); both species lacked long‑term photoreceptor preservation after functional restoration. Daluwatumulle et al. 2026 found moderate-to-high molecular concordance for many canine cancer models but with large variation across tumor types (model robustness scores 31.1%–85.05%, normalized per‑gene distances 0.007–0.047 and mean sample–sample correlation differences ~0.1007), indicating dogs can mirror human cancer molecular profiles for some tumors but not uniformly.
why_range_is_wide: The wide range (≈31%–85% robustness) reflects variation by cancer type and inclusion of deliberate negative controls; additionally the two studies measure different outcomes (functional therapeutic rescue in RPE65 therapy versus transcriptomic/molecular concordance across cancers), so values arise from distinct sub‑analyses and are not directly comparable.
negative_controls: Daluwatumulle et al. 2026 flagged negative controls with low scores: adrenocortical carcinoma (Adult 31.1%, Pediatric 33.56%) and adult leukemia (Leukemia (Adult) 40.31%, LAML noted as low).
